surface_summary: The cases appear as a series of complex murders and disappearances involving high society and servants, with multiple suspects and conflicting testimonies. Lady Molly Robertson-Kirk, a female detective at Scotland Yard, investigates each case using intuition and undercover work. The public and police initially accept various theories, but the truth is revealed through Lady Molly's persistent efforts.
accepted_facts: Captain Hubert de Mazareen was convicted of murdering Mr. Steadman.
Mr. Philip Baddock had motives related to inheritance and was involved in forgery.
Lady Irene Culledon was present at the time of her husband's death and had a large hat.
Miss Cruikshank impersonated a charwoman and was involved in Mrs. Dunstan's murder.
inferred_conclusions: Captain Hubert de Mazareen was guilty of murder.
Lady Irene Culledon was innocent and merely a grieving widow.
Miss Cruikshank was a loyal servant falsely accused.
mechanism_description: Philip Baddock and his accomplice Felkin orchestrated the murder of Mr. Steadman to secure a forged will favoring Baddock, using a staged breakdown and a planted murder weapon to implicate Captain de Mazareen. Lady Irene Culledon poisoned her husband Mark Culledon with morphia in a public café to prevent scandal and secure inheritance. Miss Cruikshank murdered Mrs. Dunstan by impersonating a charwoman and using a bag of sand to incapacitate her before asphyxiation, motivated by greed and blackmail.
delivery_path: Philip Baddock and Felkin forged a will in a darkened room with Mr. Steadman.
They sabotaged the car to force Mr. Steadman to walk through the woods.
Felkin murdered Mr. Steadman with a stick and planted the weapon near the body.
Captain de Mazareen was framed by being last seen with Mr. Steadman and carrying the stick.
Lady Irene Culledon administered morphia in chocolate at Mathis’ café and left the victim unattended.
Miss Cruikshank disguised herself as a charwoman, incapacitated Mrs. Dunstan with a blow from a bag of sand, and asphyxiated her with gas.
Lady Molly uncovered the truth through disguise, interrogation, and gathering of physical evidence.
outcome_result: The true culprits were exposed, Captain Hubert de Mazareen was pardoned, and justice was served through Lady Molly’s investigations.

false_assumption.statement: Captain Hubert de Mazareen was guilty of murdering Mr. Steadman.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: He was the last person seen with the victim and was found with the murder weapon. The circumstantial evidence and his silence about his whereabouts made him the prime suspect.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The actual murder was committed by Philip Baddock and Felkin who cleverly framed de Mazareen using forged documents and planted evidence.

supporting_points: He was last seen with the victim before the murder.
The murder weapon was identified as his property.
He had no alibi for the time of the murder.
There was circumstantial evidence of motive related to inheritance.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The evidence was planted and the forged will was the true motive behind the murder, implicating others.

red_herrings.description: Lady Irene Culledon appeared as a grieving widow and was initially suspected due to her presence and the large hat worn at the crime scene.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was motivated by jealousy and inheritance but did not commit the murder; her large hat was a misidentification factor.

red_herrings.description: Miss Cruikshank was seen as a loyal servant and victim of circumstances, but her behavior was suspicious.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was actually the murderer, using disguise and blackmail to cover her crime.

closed_circle.rationale: All suspects had access, motive, and opportunity; the investigation focused on these individuals due to their relationships with victims and involvement in the events.

time_windows: Night of January 23rd for Mary Nicholls disappearance
Christmas Eve night for Major Ceely murder
Evening of April 1904 for Mr. Steadman murder
Early morning hours for Mrs. Dunstan murder

inference_path.observation: Captain Hubert de Mazareen was last seen with Mr. Steadman and carried a stick found near the murder scene.
inference_path.correction: The stick was planted by Felkin, who also cut his own hand to stain it.
inference_path.effect: De Mazareen was framed for the murder.
required_evidence: Testimony of chauffeur George Taylor about car breakdown and walking through woods
Confession of Mr. Felkin about planting the stick and murder

inference_path.observation: Lady Irene Culledon wore a large hat similar to the one described by witnesses at Mathis’ café.
inference_path.correction: The hat was specially ordered and worn only once on the day of the murder.
inference_path.effect: Identified Lady Irene as the woman in the big hat and murderer.
required_evidence: Testimony of maid about hat order and wearing
Waitresses’ identification and contradictory statements about the hat

inference_path.observation: Miss Cruikshank was a loyal servant and victim of circumstances.
inference_path.correction: She impersonated Mrs. Thomas and murdered Mrs. Dunstan using a bag of sand and gas.
inference_path.effect: Revealed Miss Cruikshank as the murderer.
required_evidence: Discovery of disguise clothes in coal cellar

inference_path.observation: Mr. Philip Baddock was a wealthy relative with motive for murder.
inference_path.correction: He conspired with Felkin to forge a will and murder Mr. Steadman.
inference_path.effect: Exposed Baddock as mastermind behind Steadman’s murder.
required_evidence: Confession of Felkin detailing the conspiracy
Discovery of forged will and related documents

inference_path.observation: Mary Nicholls was murdered at Ash Court.
inference_path.correction: Her sister Susan was the actual victim, impersonating Mary to meet Lord Edbrooke, who murdered Susan.
inference_path.effect: Changed victim identity and revealed motive of blackmail and murder.
required_evidence: Confession of Mary Nicholls about her disappearance
Admission of Lord Edbrooke’s involvement and subsequent suicide

inference_path.observation: Jane Turner was assaulted by an elderly woman and a man.
inference_path.correction: Jane Turner alone staged the assault and blackmail scheme to extort money from the Countess of Hohengebirg.
inference_path.effect: Revealed Jane Turner as sole perpetrator of the assault and blackmail.
required_evidence: Jane Turner’s confession and attempted suicide
Letter from Jane Turner to the Countess

inference_path.correction: Leonard disguised himself as his sister Olive and maid Rosie Campbell to commit robberies and evade capture.
inference_path.effect: Explained disappearance and criminal activities as a disguise scheme.
required_evidence: Witness statements about contradictory sightings of Olive and Rosie
Lady Molly’s undercover observation and note exchanges

discriminating_test.design: Lady Molly arranged for the maids of Lady Irene Culledon to wear large hats, including the one worn on the murder day, and paraded them before the Mathis’ café waitress who identified the mysterious woman. This test aimed to confirm if the waitress could reliably identify the murderer by the hat and stature.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The waitress’s identification of the hat and wearer confirmed Lady Irene Culledon as the woman in the big hat and the murderer of Mark Culledon.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The waitress consistently identifies the same hat and wearer among several candidates, eliminating doubt about the murderer’s identity.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of characters, their motives, and timelines. Lady Molly’s intuitive deductions are based on clues such as the unique large hat, forged documents, and contradictory witness statements, all presented in the narrative. The disguised identities and planted evidence are foreshadowed through inconsistencies and testimonies, allowing an attentive reader to piece together the true culprits and their methods.
